name: Shoal Meridian
geological_features: Vast tidal flats stretching hundreds of kilometers at the equator
Shallow inland seas connected by braided river deltas
Eroded sandstone mesas rising from wetland basins
specific_features: Migratory megafauna herds visible from orbit as dark ribbons crossing the flats
The Meridian Line — a planetary-scale algal bloom that traces the equator in vivid green
description: Shoal Meridian is a medium terrestrial world defined by its extraordinary flatness and the dominance of shallow water across nearly sixty percent of its surface. Tidal flats extend to the horizon in every direction, their surfaces shimmering with thin sheets of water that advance and retreat with the pull of three small moons. The sandstone mesas that punctuate the wetlands are the only true highlands, their flat tops hosting dense thickets of wind-sculpted vegetation.

The atmosphere carries the perpetual smell of wet earth and salt, a rich organic perfume that intensifies during the twice-daily tidal surges. Light refracts through the shallow water layers to cast rippling patterns across everything, giving the landscape a dreamlike, shifting quality that disoriented early survey teams. Birdsong — or its alien equivalent — fills the air at dawn and dusk, a cacophony of clicks and whistles from creatures that have never known silence.

The megafauna of Shoal Meridian follow ancient migration routes across the flats, their paths so consistent they have worn visible grooves into the sediment over geological time. Xenobiologists believe the herds navigate by sensing the planet's magnetic field, which is unusually strong and regular for a world this size. The algal bloom known as the Meridian Line appears to be symbiotic with the migratory species, flourishing in their wake.

Several colonial ventures have expressed interest in Shoal Meridian's biomass potential and pharmaceutical-grade flora, but the Colonial Conservation Bureau has imposed a Category Three protection order citing the complexity and fragility of the tidal ecosystem. Unauthorized harvesting operations have been intercepted twice in the past decade, and a permanent orbital monitoring station now watches over the world's shallow, teeming waters.
